title: Experimental quantum telecloning across silicon photonic chips
authors: Zicong Wen, Kai Wang, Bochi Wu, Leizhen Chen, Yan-Qing Lu, Shining Zhu, Xiao-Song Ma
abstract: Telecloning -- the combination of quantum teleportation and cloning -- offers a powerful mechanism to disseminate unknown quantum states to multiple spatially separated recipients with optimal fidelity. Despite its conceptual importance for quantum networks, an experimental demonstration of symmetric qubit quantum telecloning remains elusive, particularly due to the challenges of generating multipartite entangled resource states and implementing stable multi-photon interference across distributed nodes. Here, we realize the optimal 1 to 2 symmetric quantum telecloning using a scalable silicon photonic platform. We implement a six-photon protocol using two independent, fiber-linked photonic chips: one generating a heralded input state and the other preparing a four-photon entangled resource state. By performing an interchip Bell-state measurement, we successfully distribute the input state into two optimal clones at remote nodes. We observe an interchip cloning fidelity of 78.45 $\pm$ 1.39%, exceeding the classical limit of 2/3 by 8 standard deviations. Our results demonstrate the robust generation and manipulation of complex multi-photon states between integrated chips, providing a foundational building block for large-scale multi-party quantum networks.
summary: The paper reports an experimental realization of optimal symmetric quantum telecloning using two interconnected silicon photonic chips. By implementing a six-photon protocol involving interchip Bell-state measurements, the researchers successfully cloned an unknown quantum state to two remote nodes. This achievement demonstrates robust multi-photon state manipulation on integrated photonics, providing a crucial building block for large-scale quantum networks.
main_problem: The primary goal was to experimentally demonstrate optimal symmetric quantum telecloning ($1 	o 2$) for unknown quantum states across spatially separated nodes.
main_result: The authors successfully achieved this using integrated silicon photonics, measuring an interchip cloning fidelity of $78.45 \pm 1.39\%$, which significantly surpasses the classical limit of $2/3$.
method: The protocol combines quantum teleportation and cloning, utilizing a six-photon setup involving two independent, fiber-linked photonic chips.
model_or_system: The experiment is performed on a scalable silicon photonic platform, employing nanowire photon-pair sources and an interchip Bell-state measurement (BSM) to distribute the input state into two optimal clones.
key_observables: Interchip cloning fidelity ($78.45 \pm 1.39\%$), resource state purity ($81.12 \pm 0.26\%$ for interchip), and reconstructed density matrices for various clone states.
important_parameters: The achieved fidelity exceeds the classical limit by 8 standard deviations; the setup involves a six-photon protocol using two chips.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on quantum state tomography performed on post-selected coincidences correlated with BSM results, and future work requires active feed-forward operation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the $1 	o 2$ telecloning schematic (Fig. 1a) and photonic chip layout (Fig. 1b). Other figures detail HHOM interference results (Fig. 2) and summarize clone state fidelities across different input states (Fig. 3, Fig. 10-16).
paper_structure: The paper systematically presents the protocol setup using integrated photonics, details component characterization (BSM visibility, resource state fidelity), reports quantitative measurements of the cloning process for various input states, and concludes by confirming performance against theoretical bounds.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it pushes the boundaries of photonic quantum information processing by demonstrating complex multi-photon entanglement distribution and state manipulation across integrated chips, a key requirement for scalable quantum networks.

S3) generates a photon pair, routing directs one photon to either U1 or U2 and the other to either U3 or U4. As a result, emission events from S2 and S3 are placed into a path superposition.
